lessons.title: Running a Python script
lessons.summary: A script is a text file of Python code. python3 runs it.

blocks.text:
A Python script is a plain text file, usually ending in `.py`, full of Python code. You don't open it like a document; you hand it to the Python interpreter, which reads it top to bottom and runs it. Anything the script prints shows up in your terminal.

On Geiss-01 there are two kinds of Python. `python3` is the system's own Python and is always there. `python` (and a fuller `python3`) appear once you load anaconda with `module load anaconda`. More on that choice two lessons from now.

command.name: python3
command.what: Runs the script. Your prompt comes back when it finishes. `python3 --version` tells you which version you have.

example.out:
Hello from Geiss-01
Python is working.
example.note: `cat hello.py` would show you the code. `python3 hello.py` runs it.

files.~/scripts/hello.py:
print("Hello from Geiss-01")
print("Python is working.")

blocks.tip: `cat` shows what a script will do before you run it. It's a good habit with any script someone hands you.

quiz.q: You have `count.py` in the folder you're in. How do you run it?
quiz.why: python3 runs the code in the file. cat only shows the code; typing the bare name only works for a script made executable (a later lesson).

lessons.title: Arguments, usage lines and tracebacks
lessons.summary: Tell a script which file to work on, and read what it says when something goes wrong.

blocks.text:
Most useful scripts work on a file you name: `python3 count_residues.py inputs/target.fasta`. Everything after the script's name is an argument, passed to the script (inside it, they are in `sys.argv`). Paths work the same as for any command: relative to the folder you're in.

If you leave a required argument out, a well-written script prints a usage line and stops. Square brackets mean optional; plain words are what you must supply. Most scripts also answer `-h` with a short help page.

example.out:
usage: count_residues.py [-h] fasta
count_residues.py: error: the following arguments are required: fasta
example.note: It wants one thing after its name: a FASTA file.

blocks.text: When a script crashes, Python prints a traceback. Read it from the bottom up. The last line says what went wrong; the line above it shows the code that failed; above that is the file name and line number.

example.out:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "top_designs.py", line 8, in <module>
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: float(r["pLDDT"]), reverse=True)
KeyError: 'pLDDT'
example.note: KeyError: the script looked up a column called `pLDDT`, and scores.csv doesn't have one. The fault is on line 8.

flags: A file or folder in the path doesn't exist. Check spelling and where you are.
This Python doesn't have a package the script imports. Wrong Python, or a missing environment.
The script looked for something (a column, an item) that isn't in the data.
The code itself is broken, often from an edit.

quiz.q: A traceback ends with `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'inputs/targt.fasta'`. What is the likely fix?
options: Fix the spelling of the file name
quiz.why: The file it was told to open doesn't exist; 'targt' is a typo. ls inputs/ shows the real name.

lessons.title: Which Python? Packages and environments
lessons.summary: System python3 versus anaconda's Python, and why imports fail.

blocks.text:
A script's `import` lines name the packages it needs: `import pandas`, `from Bio import SeqIO`. Each Python on the server has its own set of packages, and a script only works with a Python that has everything it imports.

The system `python3` (/usr/bin/python3) has only Python's standard library: csv, json, os, sys, math and friends. `module load anaconda` adds anaconda's Python, which also has numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy and Biopython (`Bio`). The design tools each have their own conda environment (`conda activate proteinmpnn`, `chai`, `rfd4`) with exactly what that tool needs.

example.out:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "gc_content.py", line 3, in <module>
    from Bio import SeqIO
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'Bio'
example.note: Nothing is wrong with the script. This Python just doesn't have Biopython.

command.name: which
command.what: Shows the path of the Python a name points to: /usr/bin/python3 for the system one, /opt/conda/... for anaconda's or a conda environment's.

try.text: `gc_content.py` needs Biopython. Run it, see it fail, load anaconda, and run it again.

files.~/proj/gc_content.py:
"""GC content of every sequence in a FASTA file, with Biopython."""
import sys
from Bio import SeqIO
from Bio.SeqUtils import gc_fraction

for record in SeqIO.parse(sys.argv[1], "fasta"):
    print(f"{record.id}\t{len(record.seq)} bp\tGC {gc_fraction(record.seq) * 100:.1f}%")

"""GC content of every sequence in a FASTA file, with Biopython."""
import sys
from Bio import SeqIO
from Bio.SeqUtils import gc_fraction

for record in SeqIO.parse(sys.argv[1], "fasta"):
    print(f"{record.id}\t{len(record.seq)} bp\tGC {gc_fraction(record.seq) * 100:.1f}%")

tasks.text: Run the script again so it works

try.hint: python3 gc_content.py genes.fasta, module load anaconda, python gc_content.py genes.fasta

blocks.warn: You can't `pip install` into the system Python on a shared server, and you shouldn't need to. Load anaconda, or ask for a conda environment.

quiz.q: A script fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'`. What do you try first?
options: Edit the script to remove the import
module load anaconda, then run it with python
quiz.why: pandas is there, just not in the system Python. anaconda's Python has it.

lessons.title: Scripts as programs: ./, > and jobs
lessons.summary: Save output, run a script by its name, and run it as a Slurm job.

blocks.text: Everything you learned about commands works for scripts too. `python3 summarize.py scores.csv > summary.txt` saves what the script prints to a file instead of the screen (`>>` adds to the end). `python3 loop.py &` runs it in the background so you get your prompt back.

A script whose first line is `#!/usr/bin/env python3` (the "shebang") can run like any program, once it is marked executable: `chmod +x filter_plddt.py`, then `./filter_plddt.py scores.csv 80`. The `./` means "the file in this folder".

example.note: This line tells the system which Python to run the file with.

blocks.text:
For anything long, run Python in a batch job like any other command. The job inherits the modules you loaded before `sbatch`, so load anaconda first if the script needs it:

`sbatch --wrap="python analyze.py scores.csv"`

or put `module load anaconda` and the python line in a job script. What the script prints goes to `slurm-JOBID.out`.

options: The file isn't marked executable; chmod +x it
quiz.why: ./NAME only runs files with the executable bit set. chmod +x filter_plddt.py fixes it (or run python3 filter_plddt.py).
